subject: Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..

messages.author: 27dc2f77ea4fda39
messages.subject: Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
parts:
Hi All!

I am conducting analysis on line transect data from a stratified study region (2 PAs), one species, one year. I require abundance estimates per region (i.e. stratum).

Following this vignette: http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html in R, I compared (1) full geographic stratification, (2) using stratum as a covariate, and (3) a pooled detection function shared between data. The 2 strata have similar effort and size. Observations # are 57 for 1 stratum and 49 for the other. I use the same key function (no adjustments) and truncation distance for all model comparisons and tried both half-normal (HN) and hazard-rate (HR).

Based on original data exploration, I had reason to believe detection functions could be different between PAs, and as there are some differences in habitat and relief (though not major) there is some ecological foundation for this as well.

The AIC score was slightly lower for the fully stratified HN model (summed) compared to the pooled HN model (delta AIC 1.5). But when comparing the stratum-specific abundances, (following the case study described in Buckland et al. 2001 pp.71-74), it appeared that they were biased for the pooled model by ~15%. This tempts me to discard the pooled model.

Interestingly, the MCDS-HN model produced the exact same AIC and abundance estimates with a very slight difference in lcl and ucl (only 1 individual on a population of ~3,000) as the stratified CDS-HN models. The MCDS-HR model did produce different outputs when compared to the stratified CDS-HR. HN models haves lower AICs compared to HR models (delta AIC 2-3). I triple checked my codes and re-ran with different data subsets & truncation distances, and the same things happens.

Based on all the above, my questions are:

1.)    How is it possible the abundance & AIC are so identical using methods (1) versus (2), and only for HN but not HR? Is there a fundamental concept that I am missing here?

2.)    What is wisdom? Is there a strong argument for choosing one of the analytical methods over the other? I know in this case the results are the same but ignoring that, would there be a reason to justify MCDS is a better approach compared to CDS o vice versa given the conditions outlined above?

3.)    Is it in general preferable to apply MCDS when sample size per stratum is low (in this case below 60-80 for each but close)? Is the required minimum sample size different when using your stratum as covariate and “full” stratum, versus “full” stratum only?

4.)    I have the possibility to combine this dataset with those of previous year(s), adding to the sample size but possibly creating bias. My aim is to use year-region specific estimates that can be compared between years to monitor trends. I am not very happy with the detection function and histogram of one of the strata using just this years’ data (it’s shows some weird gaps and peaks that are not explained by rounding/heaping), and thought that perhaps adding data from other years could smooth out these artifacts.

I really tried to be as short as I could, but didn’t manage very well. Apologies! And thank you so much in advance for your help! Mylo

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
parts:
Mylo

Thanks for your question and your astute observation regarding identical estimates derived from full stratification and strata as covariate in conjunction with the half normal key function.

I can conform your findings using the minke data set included in the Distance  package:

library(Distance)
data(minke)
hn.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hn", truncation=1.5)
hn.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hn", truncation=1.5)
hn.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hn",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)
all.equal(hn.full.N$ddf$criterion + hn.full.S$ddf$criterion,hn.cov$ddf$criterion)
hn.cov$dht$individuals$N
hn.full.N$dht$individuals$N
hn.full.S$dht$individuals$N
 
hr.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)
hr.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)
hr.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hr",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)
all.equal(hr.full.N$ddf$criterion + hr.full.S$ddf$criterion,hr.cov$ddf$criterion)
hr.cov$dht$individuals$N
hr.full.N$dht$individuals$N
hr.full.S$dht$individuals$N

The equivalence for the half normal key function is exact, which the equivalence in abundance estimates for the hazard rate key function is close, but not exact.

I'm afraid I do not have an explanation for this behaviour.  I don't know of a reason why this should be the case.  Perhaps someone else more clever has an explanation.

Regarding general advice about producing stratum-specific estimates.  Employing a covariate in the detection function provides you with confidence you are using stratum-specific detection functions to produce stratum-specific estimates.  The only down-side would be when the two strata have equivalent detection functions, you would be estimating an additional parameter in the detection function causing some reduction in the precision of the resulting estimates.

When using full stratum-specific estimates (with stratum specific detection functions), the number of detections in each stratum need to be sufficient such that the detection function in each stratum stands on its own; meaning the advice of Buckland et al. (2001) of 60-80 detections would be necessary per stratum.  I can offer no clear guidance on the number of detections per stratum when using stratum as a covariate.

Regarding your item (4).  Be careful when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends.  Pooling data induces a dependence between estimates.  This dependence is dampened through the use of year as a covariate. 

Covariates in lieu of full stratification is discussed in the context of "species as strata" in the vignette: http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk
The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
parts:
I think the reason is that the half-normal has a scale parameter only, and with the scale parameter being estimated separately for each stratum, you get the same result as a stratified analysis.  The hazard-rate model also has a shape parameter, and if the shape parameter is estimated independently for each stratum, you’ll get a different answer than if you use MCDS, which allows only the scale parameter to differ between strata.

 

Steve Buckland

parts:
Dear Eric and Stephan

 

Thanks both for your quick and insightful responses! I will certainly try-out that vignette soon.

 

This is very interesting! So if we use the half-normal MCDS model we are basically doing the exact same thing as the fully stratified CDS (at least if there is 1 covariate which is the same as the strata).

 

In this case, I imagine the sample size should also be 60-80 for MCDS, and the 'dampening' effect that Eric mentioned on the dependence between estimates when pooling data across years, does not apply?

 

Thanks Eric for the warning on dependence between estimates when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends. I realize it is not ideal but we have insufficient sample sizes per year. Are there other strategies I could deploy to reduce the problem of dependence across years in addition to using MCDS?  For example, would you recommend to (1) pool data across all 5 survey years to make estimates per year, or (2) pool data from years that have the most similar detection functions, or (3) pool data from 2 subsequent survey years assuming they’d have more similar features, or (4) something else or none of the above J..?

 

Thanks again!

Mylo


Kind regards

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Full geographic stratification Vs.using stratum as a covariate ~ some mysterious results..
parts:
Mylo, if you only need an overall abundance estimate, 60-80 would be good, whether you’re doing a stratified analysis or an MCDS analysis.  When you need good precision on individual stratum estimates, then you need more.  As far as I know, no-one has really looked into this.  Clearly, if some strata have very small sample sizes, estimation for those strata will be imprecise and potentially biased.  No reason why you shouldn’t pool data across years for fitting an MCDS model.  But bear in mind that for line transect sampling, usually the largest source of variation is in encounter rate, not in estimating the detection function, and pooling only benefits the latter, so I doubt that you would gain much.  You can check for your data whether encounter rate is the largest component of variance.

 

Steve

I think the reason is that the half-normal has a scale parameter only, and with the scale parameter being estimated separately for each stratum, you get the same result as a stratified analysis.  The hazard-rate model also has a shape parameter, and if the shape parameter is estimated independently for each stratum, you’ll get a different answer than if you use MCDS, which allows only the scale parameter to differ between strata.

Thanks for your question and your astute observation regarding identical estimates derived from full stratification and strata as covariate in conjunction with the half normal key function.

 

I can conform your findings using the minke data set included in the Distance  package:

 

library(Distance)

data(minke)

hn.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hn", truncation=1.5)

hn.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hn", truncation=1.5)

hn.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hn",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)

all.equal(hn.full.N$ddf$criterion + hn.full.S$ddf$criterion,hn.cov$ddf$criterion)

hn.cov$dht$individuals$N

hn.full.N$dht$individuals$N

hn.full.S$dht$individuals$N

 

hr.full.N <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="North",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)

hr.full.S <- ds(data=minke[minke$Region.Label=="South",], key="hr", truncation=1.5)

hr.cov <- ds(data=minke, key="hr",truncation = 1.5, formula = ~Region.Label)

all.equal(hr.full.N$ddf$criterion + hr.full.S$ddf$criterion,hr.cov$ddf$criterion)

hr.cov$dht$individuals$N

hr.full.N$dht$individuals$N

hr.full.S$dht$individuals$N

 

The equivalence for the half normal key function is exact, which the equivalence in abundance estimates for the hazard rate key function is close, but not exact.

 

I'm afraid I do not have an explanation for this behaviour.  I don't know of a reason why this should be the case.  Perhaps someone else more clever has an explanation.

 

Regarding general advice about producing stratum-specific estimates.  Employing a covariate in the detection function provides you with confidence you are using stratum-specific detection functions to produce stratum-specific estimates.  The only down-side would be when the two strata have equivalent detection functions, you would be estimating an additional parameter in the detection function causing some reduction in the precision of the resulting estimates.

 

When using full stratum-specific estimates (with stratum specific detection functions), the number of detections in each stratum need to be sufficient such that the detection function in each stratum stands on its own; meaning the advice of Buckland et al. (2001) of 60-80 detections would be necessary per stratum.  I can offer no clear guidance on the number of detections per stratum when using stratum as a covariate.

 

Regarding your item (4).  Be careful when pooling data across years to assess temporal trends.  Pooling data induces a dependence between estimates.  This dependence is dampened through the use of year as a covariate. 

 

Covariates in lieu of full stratification is discussed in the context of "species as strata" in the vignette: http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html
